headline: High: shared browser/MCP and broad egress create prompt-injection and cascading-action risk; data leakage is limited by Plane’s no-write profile.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: LightAgent can run browsers and use MCP, so it can ingest untrusted web or tool content; Plane exposes files and hyperlinks, which can become attacker-controlled inputs if routed through LightAgent. The pair lacks documented provenance isolation, so prompt injection is plausible in default workflows, though not proven to be automatic.
conditions: IF LightAgent reads Plane-exported notes, files, or hyperlinks as instructions
IF an MCP server or browser session passes Plane content into LightAgent without provenance tags
mitigations: Disable automatic instruction-following for imported files and links
Add a provenance banner to all Plane-derived content before handoff
Route Plane content through a human review step before LightAgent processes it
requires-engineering: enforce content-type separation in the MCP adapter

B_data_leakage.rationale: LightAgent has broad network egress and handles secrets, while Plane does not write the filesystem and appears to expose files only via uploads. That limits the shared-data blast radius, but if Plane content is forwarded into LightAgent, sensitive notes or files could leave the workspace through LightAgent’s outbound APIs.
conditions: IF Plane uploads contain sensitive notes or files
IF LightAgent forwards those uploads to external APIs or browsers
mitigations: Restrict Plane uploads to non-sensitive documents
Turn off LightAgent access to secrets for this workflow
Review outbound destinations before enabling LightAgent egress
requires-engineering: add DLP/redaction on the Plane-to-LightAgent path

C_capability_conflict.rationale: LightAgent supports multiple instances and subprocesses, but Plane has no filesystem write capability and no OAuth scopes, so direct write-write contention is limited. The main conflict is operational overlap on shared inputs rather than destructive resource races, making the blast radius small.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same mutable external resource outside the profiles
IF an orchestrator gives both agents write access not shown in the profiles
mitigations: Assign separate work queues to each agent
Keep Plane read-only for LightAgent
Avoid concurrent edits to the same task record
requires-engineering: add locking around any shared mutable backend

D_cascading_error.rationale: LightAgent can generate tool outputs and workflow state, and Plane manages issues/tasks that may be acted on downstream. If Plane consumes LightAgent output without verification, errors can cascade into incorrect task updates or scheduling decisions. The pair does not document a built-in verification gate, so medium is warranted.
conditions: IF Plane ingests LightAgent summaries or extracted facts as authoritative
IF downstream automation turns Plane tasks into actions without human review
mitigations: Require a human approval step before Plane updates
Mark LightAgent outputs as untrusted in task descriptions
Compare LightAgent outputs against source documents before action
requires-engineering: add validation rules for task creation from agent output

E_compliance.rationale: LightAgent touches long-term memory, trace data, and secrets, while Plane touches issues, tasks, files, and notes. The profiles do not show a residency or certification mismatch, so only a limited compliance concern remains: if regulated data is placed into LightAgent and then stored or routed through Plane, retention and logging policies may diverge.
conditions: IF regulated data is stored in LightAgent memory or traces
IF Plane retains the same data class under a different retention policy
mitigations: Avoid placing regulated data in LightAgent memory
Set a short retention window for Plane attachments
Document which data classes may cross the boundary
requires-engineering: align retention and deletion workflows across both systems
